title: The priest
hook: what he's doing at the front

segments.voice: Yesterday, pradakshina, walking the circle clockwise. Your line was around. What did you notice your day circling? Day one hundred and thirty-five.

You're standing at the threshold of the inner shrine. Inside, in the lamplight, a man in a white cloth, bare-chested, a thread across his shoulder, is moving fast. He's chanting in Sanskrit, almost too quickly to follow. He pours something over the image, picks up flowers, rings a bell, turns, and suddenly he's asking you something. Your name? He repeats it into the chant. Then flowers go up, the flame comes out, and a spoonful of water lands in your palm. It's over in two minutes, and you have no idea what just happened. Today: the priest.
screen: `A MAN IN WHITE, CHANTING FAST.` → `HE ASKS YOUR NAME.` → `WHAT JUST HAPPENED?`

segments.voice: The word is pujari: the one who does the puja. In a temple, he's usually the only one who goes into the inner shrine. He isn't a preacher, and he isn't necessarily your guru. His job is the form: the rites, done exactly, every day. His day often starts before dawn. He wakes the deity, bathes the image with water, sometimes milk, honey or other offerings, a rite called abhisheka. He dresses it, decorates it, offers food, and performs arti at set times. The day ends when he puts the deity to rest at night. Many of these rites follow detailed temple manuals, handed down over centuries. And when you come with an offering, he does something on your behalf. That's the moment in the story. He asks your name, and often your family lineage or birth star, and places them inside the Sanskrit, stating who is offering, when and where, and for what. Then he recites the names of the deity, sometimes a hundred and eight of them, offering a flower or a pinch of something with each name. That's called archana. He brings back the flame, the holy water and the prasad for you. Traditionally, most temple priests have come from Brahmin families trained from childhood, and that's still common. In recent decades, some temples and groups have also trained priests from other backgrounds, including women. Families also call a priest to their homes for weddings, naming ceremonies and housewarmings. Whatever the setting, the idea is the same. You don't have to know every word. Someone holds the form.
screen: `PUJARI — THE ONE WHO DOES THE PUJA.` · `WAKE, BATHE, DRESS, FEED, REST.` · `YOUR NAME, INSIDE THE SANSKRIT.` · `SOMEONE HOLDS THE FORM.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Think of someone who keeps a form going so others can rely on it. The person who opens the building every morning. The grandmother who never misses the evening lamp. The nurse on the night shift. The teacher who arrives early. They do it whether or not anyone notices. Picture them, doing their careful work. If you'd like, silently thank them. Then notice that you, too, hold a small form now: a corner, a flame, a practice. The bell holds the time.
Pujari. The temple priest: the one who does the puja, every day, exactly, and offers on your behalf. Today's word.
Your line: someone holds the form. Today, thank one person who keeps something going that you rely on, and tell them you noticed. Day one hundred and thirty-five.

howItsDone: In Hindu temples, the pujari performs the daily rites for the deity (bathing, dressing, food offerings and arti), and on request performs archana on a devotee's behalf, reciting the deity's names with their name and lineage; families also invite priests home for life-cycle rites.
